High-level summary
- CLIP alignment fails mainly because the prompt forces fallback/neutral tokens, forbids useful mid-confidence emissions, and prunes or delays high-value nouns/verbs (anchors, dynamic actions, signage). Fixes should increase reliable, high-saliency content (scene anchors, concrete fine-classes, motion tokens, text) while keeping anti‑hallucination guardrails.

Concrete, actionable feedback (do not rewrite the prompt; change these rules)

1) Prioritize high-value nouns and actions in assembly/pruning
- Change pruning priority so slots 1–3 (subject + micro‑action + fine‑class) cannot be removed. Rationale: CLIP strongly weights nouns/verbs; keeping them preserves alignment even at cost of background details.
- When pruning, remove adjectives/lighting/background before micro‑actions or fine classes. Benefit: preserves semantic anchors that CLIP uses.

2) Relax brittleness around MEDIUM verification for dynamic content
- Allow MEDIUM‑band emission of motion verbs (e.g., jumping, pawing, clearing, showing, speaking) when geometry OR motion_confidence + another complementary signal (saliency/segmentation) is ≥ MEDIUM. But restrict to an enumerated MEDIUM verb whitelist. Rationale: dynamic verbs boost CLIP similarity but must be constrained to avoid hallucination.

3) Expand and curate MEDIUM whitelists (fine‑class & anchors)
- Add high-utility items to MEDIUM lists: boat/shallow boat/canoe, shrine/temple/ghats/steps, children/children group, performer/chorus line, parade elements, vendor/produce stand, hedgerow/trees. Also add anchors: boats/canopies, flagpoles, marquee, ladder. Rationale: these cover frequent scene elements visible to CLIP but often fall into LOW and become generic.
- Keep these lists enumerated and limited; permit MEDIUM emission only from that list to control hallucination.

4) Make fallbacks neutral and conservative; forbid “plausible” inventing
- Replace any free fallback that suggests a specific object (e.g., “woven basket”) with neutral fallbacks like “object on table”, “storefront behind”, “boats moored beside”. Explicitly forbid substituting plausible but unverified props. Rationale: hallucinated specifics reduce CLIP match if wrong and mislead downstream.

5) First‑words constraint: allow MEDIUM-anchored subjects
- Modify “first 6–8 words” rule to accept either (a) subject + HIGH anchor OR (b) subject + MEDIUM anchor (from whitelist) by the 8th word; otherwise emit generic plural fallback. Rationale: avoids premature generic fallbacks when useful anchor is present but detected slightly later.

6) Strengthen spatial/formation emission rules
- Require emission of explicit spatial tokens (left/right/center/foreground/background, alongside/moored beside, flanking) when geometry/segmentation indicates reliable localization. Make these MEDIUM‑eligible via a short spatial-phrase whitelist. Rationale: CLIP benefits from spatial relations that disambiguate which object text refers to.

7) OCR/signage handling improvements for CLIP
- Permit MEDIUM OCR descriptors to include short, high‑confidence partial reads (single words/letters) when OCR_confidence ≥ MEDIUM and saliency_score high; still forbid inventing or completing partial brands. Add a MEDIUM signage whitelist (e.g., “marquee above”, “large red sign upper right”, or up to 6 visible letters when OCR_confidence supports them). Rationale: visible text is highly informative for CLIP matching.

8) Improve micro‑action/contact template flexibility and verification logic
- For micro‑action slot, allow MEDIUM template forms beyond the current narrow whitelist (e.g., "left hand holding X", "pawing", "jumping at") when corresponding evidences support it. Require strict template formatting and no hedges. Rationale: more precise micro‑actions increase specificity without hallucinating.

9) Saliency tie‑breaking and ordering tweaks
- Prefer text > large object > face > clothing, but bias selection toward anchors that have high saliency even if detector_confidence is MEDIUM. Rationale: CLIP often keys on large color patches and signage.

10) Prune less aggressively on short text quotas; preserve essential tokens
- Raise soft target length slightly (e.g., target 10–16 words) or permit +2 words when including a HIGH‑verified fine class and a HIGH‑verified anchor; keep hard cap. Rationale: some real images need slightly longer captions to include anchors/signage that improve CLIP scores.

11) Tighten anti‑hallucination guardrails and validator fallback
- Keep absolute bans: no invented brands/ages/emotions/intentions. But make the final validator safe caption smarter: if MEDIUM anchors or fine classes were verified, incorporate them rather than defaulting to the generic safe tuple. Rationale: fallback often discards useful MEDIUM info and hurts CLIP.

12) Monitoring and conservative thresholds
- When loosening MEDIUM emissions, compensate by (a) requiring two complementary evidences for MEDIUM verb/class where possible, and (b) log/track cases where MEDIUM emissions later receive low CLIP—use that to iteratively prune whitelist items. Why these changes improve mean CLIP
- CLIP prefers concrete nouns and salient text/anchors and benefits from verbs that describe visible motion. The current prompt over-relies on low-evidence fallbacks and aggressively prunes/removes anchors and actions; that produces generic captions that score low. Preserving and permitting mid-confidence emissions for high-value tokens (anchors, motion verbs, signage, spatial relations), while keeping enumerated whitelists and anti‑hallucination constraints, will produce more discriminative captions that better match CLIP’s visual-text sensitivities.

Quick prioritized implementation plan
1. Adjust pruning to protect slots 1–3.
2. Expand MEDIUM whitelists (fine-class, anchors, verbs) and require complementary evidence.
3. Relax first‑words rule to accept MEDIUM anchors.
4. Improve MEDIUM OCR handling and spatial emission rules.
5. Tweak fallback vocabulary to be strictly neutral and update validator fallback to use MEDIUM info.
6. Add monitoring for MEDIUM emissions to refine whitelists.

Potential risks and mitigations
- Risk: increased hallucinations if MEDIUM lists are too permissive. Mitigate by keeping enumerated lists small, requiring two evidences where possible, and auditing low-CLIP cases.
- Risk: slightly longer captions. Mitigate by conservative target-length allowance and strict pruning of low-value descriptors.

- mean_clip and clip_win_rate (primary); mean_delta_clip.
- generic_rate (should decrease).
- false-positive hallucination rate (manually sample errors).
- mean_caption_len (ensure still reasonable).

Overall: shift the prompt from conservative, fallback-heavy behavior to a guardedly more expressive regime that elevates scene anchors, verbs, signage, and spatial relations when supported by evidence. This will increase discriminative content that CLIP can match, raising the primary metric while keeping hallucination risk controlled.

High-level summary
- The prompt already targets CLIP‑salient cues (OCR, large props, counts, dominant objects) but is overly complex, sometimes internally inconsistent, and brittle: many rules conflict (first‑words constraint + strict slot preservation + tight length caps), causing validation rewrites and lower CLIP scores. Simplify and make deterministic decision/priority logic explicit, reduce ambiguity about verification bands, and codify which tokens are highest value for CLIP so the captioner reliably surfaces them early.

Prioritized, specific feedback (what to change and why)

1) Make the anchor priority and early‑placement rule deterministic and simpler
- Change: Explicitly require: “If OCR_med/high present → quoted OCR token first; else if large prop/signage → name prop; else people/faces → ‘group of people’ or fine class; else use neutral anchor.” State a single tie‑break scoring (OCR > prop area > detector confidence > color patch area).
- Why: CLIP strongly benefits from early unique tokens (text, unique props). A deterministic rule prevents ambiguous choice and ensures the first 6–8 words consistently contain discriminative tokens, improving alignment.

2) Replace loose “verification band” language with actionable gating logic
- Change: Map detector outputs to clear gating actions in the prompt (example: “if OCR_conf ≥ 0.85 → emit full quoted text and placement; elif 0.50 ≤ OCR_conf < 0.85 → emit one quoted token ≤6 chars and placement only if saliency_score ≥ threshold; else → neutral anchor fallback”). Do same for segmentation_iou and detector_count_confidence.
- Why: The current bands are fine but vague for implementation. Explicit if/elif rules reduce ambiguity and prevent accidental emission of low‑confidence hallucinations.

3) Tighten OCR instructions and require placement + saliency metadata
- Change: Require placement phrase whenever OCR is quoted (e.g., "on wall left"), and limit MEDIUM OCR to emit only if a saliency metric (area or contrast) exceeds a threshold. For partial OCR, mandate “do not complete or guess” and fall back to neutral anchor.
- Why: Quoted text is extremely discriminative for CLIP but dangerous when mis‑transcribed; placement helps CLIP tie text to image region.

4) Simplify and harden the First‑Words rule and fallback minimal template
- Change: Recast first‑words rule as: “Within first 8 words, emit [subject group token] + [anchor token]. If no MEDIUM/HIGH anchor exists, use deterministic minimal form: ‘group of people, storefront behind, right hand near object, people/dogs/vehicles/vendor stand.’” Make the minimal form explicit and shorter.
- Why: Current spec forces an auto‑rewrite but is underspecified; making the fallback deterministic and explicit avoids divergent rewrites and improves consistency.

5) Make the micro‑action slot builder less brittle and tied to evidence
- Change: Keep “always emit micro‑action” but rephrase to: “Choose the highest evidence template available (HIGH exact template, else MEDIUM whitelist verb, else LOW fallback ‘[part] near [object]’). Allow short orientation tokens (‘back view’, ‘seen from behind’) under MEDIUM as an allowed micro‑action adjunct.”
- Why: Enforcing the highest evidence available prevents the model from using MEDIUM verbs when no evidence supports them (reducing hallucination) and increases alignment with detectors.

6) Prioritize CLIP‑salient tokens in pruning, not just slots 1–3
- Change: Update pruning priority list to keep OCR tokens, anchor nouns, verified counts, unique color/clothing tokens before any adjectives or background info. Explicitly prohibit pruning of any token that was used to satisfy a verification rule (OCR, MEDIUM/HIGH anchor, verified count).
- Why: CLIP gains from unique nouns and text; previous pruning order might delete these.

7) Make count emission rules explicit and conservative
- Change: Only emit digits when detector_count_confidence ≥ 0.70. If close but not meeting threshold, use “several” or “a few” should be banned — instead use plural fallbacks (people, items) to avoid weak quantifiers. If zero is strongly indicated, allow “none”.
- Why: Miscounting harms CLIP if the caption mentions a wrong numeral; being conservative reduces incorrect specifics.

8) Reduce complexity of the MEDIUM whitelist and whitelist tokens
- Change: Keep the whitelist but reduce its size and show exact allowed placements in examples (e.g., “’red patterned dress’ only emit under MEDIUM and only in the clothing slot”). Explicitly forbid using whitelist tokens anywhere except the specified slot positions.
- Why: Prevents accidental use of whitelist words in other slots (which violated the validator in examples).

9) Add short deterministic anti‑hallucination replacement rules
- Change: If any requested detail cannot be verified at MEDIUM/HIGH, replace with an explicit neutral fallback phrasing (list the allowed fallback tokens). Put this block near the top of the prompt so the generator applies it first.
- Why: Reduces speculative claims that lower CLIP similarity and produce wrong specifics.

- Change: Add examples that show: (a) OCR_HIGH → full quoted text + placement; (b) PROP_MED → anchor early; (c) PEOPLE_MED → subject+anchor early; (d) LOW evidence → minimal safe caption; (e) pruning example where adjectives are removed but anchor retained; (f) count emission when detector_conf high.
- Why: Models and downstream implementers learn rules best from concrete before/after pairs. They also help debugging.

11) Improve validation logging and diagnostics
- Change: Require captions to emit a short, internal, non‑visible debug token or flag (for training/debug only) that records which verification band(s) were used (OCR_MED, SEG_HIGH, COUNT_OK). Alternatively, mandate the system logs these decisions server‑side. Also require the auto‑rewrite to output a code indicating which rule triggered the rewrite.
- Why: This will let you analyze frequent failure modes and refine thresholds to maximize CLIP alignment.

12) Soften or relax the hard length caps slightly
- Change: Allow length cap to be expanded by +2 words more often when a MEDIUM anchor plus a MEDIUM micro‑action are present. Or, better, change the target from word count to tokenized length threshold excluding required slots.
- Why: The current caps force deletion of discriminative adjectives and sometimes require rewriting; a small, controlled relaxation keeps salient tokens and improves CLIP score.

13) Remove or clarify overlapping “never prune slots 1–3” + “preserve MEDIUM tokens” constraints
- Change: Explicitly state that slots 1–3 are immutable only for tokens that were verified at MEDIUM/HIGH; otherwise they may be replaced with the neutral fallback. Give a deterministic order when multiple MEDIUM tokens compete (use anchor priority).
- Why: Current instruction can be inconsistent when no medium/high tokens exist; clarification avoids failing final validator.

14) Add explicit guidance to prefer unique/rare nouns and adjectives that CLIP weights highly
- Change: Encourage emission of unique nouns (e.g., “marquee”, “bench”, “table”, “red railing”) and single distinctive colors when verified. Prohibit vague composite phrases (“people/dogs/vehicles/vendor stand”) unless no verified fine class exists.
- Why: CLIP responds better to unique, concrete tokens than to vague collections.

15) Test harness / evaluation protocol suggestions
- Change: Require batch evaluation on held‑out images with measured delta_clip after any prompt change. Use targeted subsets (OCR‑heavy images, signage images, small object images) to ensure changes improve mean_clip across modes.
- Why: Prevents overfitting to one image type and ensures improvements generalize.

Potential pitfalls to avoid
- Overly many interlocking rules will make the captioner brittle; prefer a small set of deterministic rules with clear priorities.
- Don’t rely purely on detector thresholds without combining a saliency metric (area/contrast) — small OCR fragments may have high confidence but low saliency.
- Avoid soft language like “prefer” — make choices deterministic to ensure the same output for the same inputs.

Short implementation checklist to incorporate into the prompt (for the optimizer to convert)
- Deterministic anchor priority ordered and enforced.
- If/elif gating for OCR/segmentation/count with explicit actions per gate.
- Exact micro‑action selection algorithm tied to highest evidence.
- Explicit minimal fallback caption template.
- Pruning rules that preserve OCR, anchors, counts.
- A small set (6–8) of annotated exemplar before/after captions.
- Diagnostics/logging hooks for rewrites and verification bands.

How these changes will improve mean_clip
- By forcing discriminative, image‑unique tokens (OCR, prop nouns, verified counts, colors) early in the caption and removing speculative content, generated captions will better match CLIP’s embedding priorities. Deterministic rules reduce inconsistent outputs and enable targeted tuning of thresholds that maximize image/text similarity.
